boj-2026-09.standing: Japan's central bank, which sets the short-term policy rate at scheduled meetings through the year. Because Japanese money has been the world's cheapest for decades, what it decides prices borrowing well beyond Japan.
boj-2026-09.recent: A generation of cross-border borrowing was built on the assumption that yen funding is free, and this is the meeting that withdraws it — the 31-year mark is the whole point. Positions financed in Tokyo and parked abroad have to be unwound back into yen, and Japan's own debt service rises with every step the committee takes.

uk-cpi-2026-10.standing: The UK's monthly consumer price index, compiled by the Office for National Statistics. It is the measure the Bank of England's inflation target is written against, and it feeds index-linked gilts, pensions and a range of regulated prices.
uk-cpi-2026-10.recent: This release settles what UK consumer prices did in September, in a single figure published in one go. Nothing on the record yet marks it out from a routine month.

fomc-2026-10.standing: The Federal Open Market Committee, which meets eight times a year to set the US federal funds rate — the overnight price of money that anchors American credit. Because the dollar prices much of the world's trade and debt, the decision travels well past US borders.
fomc-2026-10.recent: The committee hiked 12-0 in September, defying Trump's calls to lower rates, and the cause was a closed strait rather than domestic demand: Houthis captured Yemen's port of Mocha, oil ran to $105, and August consumer prices rose 0.4%. October settles whether the Fed keeps tightening into a supply shock it cannot reach.

ecb-2026-10.standing: The European Central Bank's Governing Council, which sets the main refinancing and deposit rates for the twenty countries sharing the euro. Its decisions set borrowing costs for roughly 350 million people and transmit through banks rather than bond markets.
ecb-2026-10.recent: The council meets with an energy shock working through wages and contracts rather than fading: Deutsche Bank has already raised where it expects the tightening to stop, to 2.75%. What the committee has to settle is whether second-round transmission — the shock passing from fuel into everything priced off it — has begun, and the euro area imports the crude that sat near $110 a barrel. The decision lands after the Fed moved 12-0 and the Bank of Japan went to a 31-year high.

boj-2026-10.standing: Japan's central bank, whose policy board sets the short-term rate eight times a year. Because yen borrowing has underpinned leveraged positions worldwide for decades, its decisions price risk far beyond Japan.
boj-2026-10.recent: The board raised the policy rate to 1.25% in September, a 31-year high, and the yen fell rather than rose — markets read the move as too small to close the gap. October's meeting tests how far the board will go against a weak currency it is also trying to defend with pension money, and every further step raises the servicing cost of the developed world's largest public debt.

boe-2026-11.standing: The Bank of England's Monetary Policy Committee, which sets Bank Rate — the rate under mortgage and borrowing costs across the UK. It meets eight times a year and members vote individually, so the split is read as closely as the decision.
boe-2026-11.recent: The committee meets after the Fed raised rates on a 12-0 vote and the Bank of Japan took its policy rate to a 31-year high, both tightening into a supply shock rather than through it — the cause named in Washington was a closed strait, with Brent near $110 a barrel. What this meeting settles is whether an imported energy shock is one to lean against too.

fomc-2026-12.standing: The Federal Open Market Committee, which meets eight times a year to set the federal funds rate that anchors the cost of dollar credit. It prices mortgages and business loans at home, and debt owed in dollars everywhere else.
fomc-2026-12.recent: September's hike was unanimous, 12-0, and the cause was a closed strait rather than a hot labour market — tightening into a supply shock policy cannot reach. August consumer prices rose 0.4% as the war arrived in the price index, and the vote came over Trump's calls to lower rates. December settles whether the committee keeps paying twice.

g20-2026-miami.standing: The annual meeting of heads of state and government from the world's largest economies, plus the European Union. It has no treaty powers, so its weight rests on what the leaders in the room agree to say and do together on debt, trade, energy and war.

ecb-2026-12.standing: The European Central Bank's Governing Council, which sets a single interest rate for every economy that uses the euro and meets roughly every six weeks. One decision in Frankfurt reaches mortgages and business credit across the whole bloc.
ecb-2026-12.recent: The tightening under way is an energy story: with Brent crude near $110 a barrel, the argument inside the Council is over second-round transmission — whether a supply shock it cannot reach has started leaking into wages and services. Deutsche Bank has already raised its ECB peak to 2.75%, and this meeting is where that path is tested.

boe-2026-12.standing: The Bank of England's Monetary Policy Committee, nine members who meet eight times a year to set Bank Rate. That rate sets what British households pay on mortgages and what the government pays to borrow, and sterling trades on its decisions.
boe-2026-12.recent: The committee's December meeting follows a quarter in which the major central banks moved the other way: the Federal Reserve raised rates 12-0 in a decision it tied to a closed strait, the Bank of Japan took its policy rate to a 31-year high, and the 10-year Treasury yield reached 5%. With Brent near $110 a barrel, the question is how much of an imported energy shock the committee treats as passing through.

boj-2026-12.standing: The Bank of Japan's policy board, which meets eight times a year to set Japan's short-term rate. Because global investors borrow cheaply in yen to buy assets elsewhere, a decision in Tokyo prices funding far beyond Japan.
boj-2026-12.recent: September's hike withdrew the assumption that Japanese money is free — and the yen fell rather than rose, which markets read as insufficient. December's decision meets a currency weak enough that Tokyo is weighing pension money as a defence, and a debt-service bill on the developed world's largest public debt that rises with every further step.
